{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the hit cap is counted before the branch-scope filter — the default scope under-delivers and pages O(n²)**

`seeRecord` stops at `query.maxHits` hits in `_hits`, but `finish()` only then filters to the active branch. Since `branch` is the **default** scope, every match on an abandoned fork consumes budget and can trigger a premature `result cap` that returns far fewer than 40 branch hits — or zero — while reporting `truncated: true`. Worse, the continuation token skips records globally, so each next page re-scans the entire prefix of the chain: paging through a fork-heavy giant session is O(n²) under a 10 s budget.

No test covers branch-scope + cap together (the seeded fork record doesn't match the test query, so the E4 test can't see this).

Directions: collect hits with branch membership decided at collection time where possible, or over-collect with slack and continue scanning when the branch-filtered count is below the cap; alternatively exclude non-branch hits from the cap accounting and document that a capped branch scan may re-examine fork hits on the next page.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment06.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the E5 "never a hang" guarantee is not enforceable — one record can blow the wall-clock budget**

The comment frames this cap as the E5 DoS bound, but a text-length cap is not a time bound on a backtracking regex engine (the Dart VM's `RegExp` backtracks — catastrophic patterns like `(a+)+$` over the 128 KB record are effectively unbounded). The time-budget check (`checkDeadline`) only runs **between** lines/blocks, never inside `pattern.hasMatch`, so a single pathological match on one giant record wedges the tool call — and the cancel token is not consulted during `execute` either — far beyond the promised 10 s, producing a hung agent rather than an "honest `truncated` report".

This matters more here than for a plain grep tool because the regex comes from the model itself, which routinely emits accidentally-quadratic patterns, and this PR's headline scenario is giant records.

Directions: bound the regex subject far smaller (a match over the first N KB of the record's preview-sized excerpt is enough for a pointer), or run the match in an isolate that can be abandoned on deadline expiry, or explicitly scope the E5 claim down to "budget checked between records" and cap per-record regex input accordingly.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment07.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: accumulator state grows linearly with archive size — the flat-memory claim (E4) does not hold**

`scanSessionSegment`'s doc claims "memory stays flat regardless of file size (E4)", and that is true only for the block/carry streaming. The accumulator itself retains per-record state for the whole chain: `_parentOf` for **every** record id (plus `_ordinalOf` in map mode, doubling it). For a multi-GB archive — this PR's explicit target — with a few million records this is hundreds of MB of id→parent pairs held for the entire scan, and it also accumulates identically on every continuation page.

Directions: the branch walk only needs parents of records on the leaf→root path. Since `RangedReadFileSystem` supports ranged reads, consider a two-pass approach (find the leaf in pass 1 storing only checkpoint/parent facts sparsely, then walk backwards in ranges), or keep parents only for records at/after the last observed fork, or correct the doc comment to state the linear bound honestly and decide whether it is acceptable for the E4 giant-session scenario.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment08.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: the human-readable outcome of `recordPendingWait` is constructed and then discarded**

`recordPendingWait`'s doc says failures are "REPORTED here and swallowed by the afterToolCall wrapper" — but the wrapper (`_attachObligationPendingWaits`) awaits the result and drops it on the floor: nothing is ever reported anywhere, and all the outcome strings (`'pending-wait already recorded…'`, `'did not carry a scheduled id…'`, the swallow-message) are dead text. As written, a silent permanent failure (e.g. the schedule_message result wording changes — see the regex coupling note) is indistinguishable from success.

Either log the outcome through the CLI's logger/bus inside the wrapper, or drop the return value and simplify `recordPendingWait` to `Future<void>` so the code says what it does.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment09.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: only the `result cap` stop carries a continuation token — time-budget stops cannot be paged**

`nextContinuation` is set exclusively when `_stopReason == 'result cap'`. A scan stopped by the 10 s budget mid-archive gets `truncated: true` with no token, so the model's only recourse is the footer advice to narrow with `kinds`/`before`/`after` — fine for specific queries, but for a broad recall sweep over a multi-GB chain there may be no narrowing that fits the budget, and the agent is stuck re-scanning from the start each call (where it will time out again at roughly the same place, since the skip only honors the token).

Since `_skipped` already implements absolute-record skipping, the token is computable for any clean stop: consider `nextContinuation = recordsTotal - 1` (or `recordsTotal`, boundary semantics permitting) whenever the stop was not an error, and extend the footer to offer continuation for `time budget` too.

`seeRecord` stops at `query.maxHits` hits in `_hits`, but `finish()` only then filters to the active branch. Since `branch` is the **default** scope, every match on an abandoned fork consumes budget and can trigger a premature `result cap` that returns far fewer than 40 branch hits — or zero — while reporting `truncated: true`. Worse, the continuation token skips records globally, so each next page re-scans the entire prefix of the chain: paging through a fork-heavy giant session is O(n²) under a 10 s budget.

No test covers branch-scope + cap together (the seeded fork record doesn't match the test query, so the E4 test can't see this).

Directions: collect hits with branch membership decided at collection time where possible, or over-collect with slack and continue scanning when the branch-filtered count is below the cap; alternatively exclude non-branch hits from the cap accounting and document that a capped branch scan may re-examine fork hits on the next page.

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the E5 "never a hang" guarantee is not enforceable — one record can blow the wall-clock budget**

The comment frames this cap as the E5 DoS bound, but a text-length cap is not a time bound on a backtracking regex engine (the Dart VM's `RegExp` backtracks — catastrophic patterns like `(a+)+$` over the 128 KB record are effectively unbounded). The time-budget check (`checkDeadline`) only runs **between** lines/blocks, never inside `pattern.hasMatch`, so a single pathological match on one giant record wedges the tool call — and the cancel token is not consulted during `execute` either — far beyond the promised 10 s, producing a hung agent rather than an "honest `truncated` report".

This matters more here than for a plain grep tool because the regex comes from the model itself, which routinely emits accidentally-quadratic patterns, and this PR's headline scenario is giant records.

Directions: bound the regex subject far smaller (a match over the first N KB of the record's preview-sized excerpt is enough for a pointer), or run the match in an isolate that can be abandoned on deadline expiry, or explicitly scope the E5 claim down to "budget checked between records" and cap per-record regex input accordingly.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment07.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: accumulator state grows linearly with archive size — the flat-memory claim (E4) does not hold**

`scanSessionSegment`'s doc claims "memory stays flat regardless of file size (E4)", and that is true only for the block/carry streaming. The accumulator itself retains per-record state for the whole chain: `_parentOf` for **every** record id (plus `_ordinalOf` in map mode, doubling it). For a multi-GB archive — this PR's explicit target — with a few million records this is hundreds of MB of id→parent pairs held for the entire scan, and it also accumulates identically on every continuation page.

Directions: the branch walk only needs parents of records on the leaf→root path. Since `RangedReadFileSystem` supports ranged reads, consider a two-pass approach (find the leaf in pass 1 storing only checkpoint/parent facts sparsely, then walk backwards in ranges), or keep parents only for records at/after the last observed fork, or correct the doc comment to state the linear bound honestly and decide whether it is acceptable for the E4 giant-session scenario.

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: only the `result cap` stop carries a continuation token — time-budget stops cannot be paged**

`nextContinuation` is set exclusively when `_stopReason == 'result cap'`. A scan stopped by the 10 s budget mid-archive gets `truncated: true` with no token, so the model's only recourse is the footer advice to narrow with `kinds`/`before`/`after` — fine for specific queries, but for a broad recall sweep over a multi-GB chain there may be no narrowing that fits the budget, and the agent is stuck re-scanning from the start each call (where it will time out again at roughly the same place, since the skip only honors the token).

Since `_skipped` already implements absolute-record skipping, the token is computable for any clean stop: consider `nextContinuation = recordsTotal - 1` (or `recordsTotal`, boundary semantics permitting) whenever the stop was not an error, and extend the footer to offer continuation for `time budget` too.

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the hit cap is counted before the branch-scope filter — the default scope under-delivers and pages O(n²)**

`seeRecord` stops at `query.maxHits` hits in `_hits`, but `finish()` only then filters to the active branch. Since `branch` is the **default** scope, every match on an abandoned fork consumes budget and can trigger a premature `result cap` that returns far fewer than 40 branch hits — or zero — while reporting `truncated: true`. Worse, the continuation token skips records globally, so each next page re-scans the entire prefix of the chain: paging through a fork-heavy giant session is O(n²) under a 10 s budget.

No test covers branch-scope + cap together (the seeded fork record doesn't match the test query, so the E4 test can't see this).

Directions: collect hits with branch membership decided at collection time where possible, or over-collect with slack and continue scanning when the branch-filtered count is below the cap; alternatively exclude non-branch hits from the cap accounting and document that a capped branch scan may re-examine fork hits on the next page.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment06.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the E5 "never a hang" guarantee is not enforceable — one record can blow the wall-clock budget**

The comment frames this cap as the E5 DoS bound, but a text-length cap is not a time bound on a backtracking regex engine (the Dart VM's `RegExp` backtracks — catastrophic patterns like `(a+)+$` over the 128 KB record are effectively unbounded). The time-budget check (`checkDeadline`) only runs **between** lines/blocks, never inside `pattern.hasMatch`, so a single pathological match on one giant record wedges the tool call — and the cancel token is not consulted during `execute` either — far beyond the promised 10 s, producing a hung agent rather than an "honest `truncated` report".

This matters more here than for a plain grep tool because the regex comes from the model itself, which routinely emits accidentally-quadratic patterns, and this PR's headline scenario is giant records.

Directions: bound the regex subject far smaller (a match over the first N KB of the record's preview-sized excerpt is enough for a pointer), or run the match in an isolate that can be abandoned on deadline expiry, or explicitly scope the E5 claim down to "budget checked between records" and cap per-record regex input accordingly.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment07.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: accumulator state grows linearly with archive size — the flat-memory claim (E4) does not hold**

`scanSessionSegment`'s doc claims "memory stays flat regardless of file size (E4)", and that is true only for the block/carry streaming. The accumulator itself retains per-record state for the whole chain: `_parentOf` for **every** record id (plus `_ordinalOf` in map mode, doubling it). For a multi-GB archive — this PR's explicit target — with a few million records this is hundreds of MB of id→parent pairs held for the entire scan, and it also accumulates identically on every continuation page.

Directions: the branch walk only needs parents of records on the leaf→root path. Since `RangedReadFileSystem` supports ranged reads, consider a two-pass approach (find the leaf in pass 1 storing only checkpoint/parent facts sparsely, then walk backwards in ranges), or keep parents only for records at/after the last observed fork, or correct the doc comment to state the linear bound honestly and decide whether it is acceptable for the E4 giant-session scenario.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment08.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: the human-readable outcome of `recordPendingWait` is constructed and then discarded**

`recordPendingWait`'s doc says failures are "REPORTED here and swallowed by the afterToolCall wrapper" — but the wrapper (`_attachObligationPendingWaits`) awaits the result and drops it on the floor: nothing is ever reported anywhere, and all the outcome strings (`'pending-wait already recorded…'`, `'did not carry a scheduled id…'`, the swallow-message) are dead text. As written, a silent permanent failure (e.g. the schedule_message result wording changes — see the regex coupling note) is indistinguishable from success.

Either log the outcome through the CLI's logger/bus inside the wrapper, or drop the return value and simplify `recordPendingWait` to `Future<void>` so the code says what it does.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment09.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: only the `result cap` stop carries a continuation token — time-budget stops cannot be paged**

`nextContinuation` is set exclusively when `_stopReason == 'result cap'`. A scan stopped by the 10 s budget mid-archive gets `truncated: true` with no token, so the model's only recourse is the footer advice to narrow with `kinds`/`before`/`after` — fine for specific queries, but for a broad recall sweep over a multi-GB chain there may be no narrowing that fits the budget, and the agent is stuck re-scanning from the start each call (where it will time out again at roughly the same place, since the skip only honors the token).

Since `_skipped` already implements absolute-record skipping, the token is computable for any clean stop: consider `nextContinuation = recordsTotal - 1` (or `recordsTotal`, boundary semantics permitting) whenever the stop was not an error, and extend the footer to offer continuation for `time budget` too.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment11.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the "no session file" degradation renders as "no records match" — the graceful-null contract is dishonest in practice**

When the host has no backing session file, this returns `truncated: false, truncationReason: 'no session file'` with zero totals. But `formatSessionSearchOutcome` only surfaces `truncationReason` when `truncated` is true, so the model actually sees:

```text

```

That claims the archive was scanned and is empty — the opposite of "this host cannot search". The tool-level null-callback branch (`'This host has no session file to search.'`) is never reached from the CLI because the callback is always `searchSessionArchive`. {"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the hit cap is counted before the branch-scope filter — the default scope under-delivers and pages O(n²)**

`seeRecord` stops at `query.maxHits` hits in `_hits`, but `finish()` only then filters to the active branch. Since `branch` is the **default** scope, every match on an abandoned fork consumes budget and can trigger a premature `result cap` that returns far fewer than 40 branch hits — or zero — while reporting `truncated: true`. Worse, the continuation token skips records globally, so each next page re-scans the entire prefix of the chain: paging through a fork-heavy giant session is O(n²) under a 10 s budget.

No test covers branch-scope + cap together (the seeded fork record doesn't match the test query, so the E4 test can't see this).

Directions: collect hits with branch membership decided at collection time where possible, or over-collect with slack and continue scanning when the branch-filtered count is below the cap; alternatively exclude non-branch hits from the cap accounting and document that a capped branch scan may re-examine fork hits on the next page.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment06.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the E5 "never a hang" guarantee is not enforceable — one record can blow the wall-clock budget**

The comment frames this cap as the E5 DoS bound, but a text-length cap is not a time bound on a backtracking regex engine (the Dart VM's `RegExp` backtracks — catastrophic patterns like `(a+)+$` over the 128 KB record are effectively unbounded). The time-budget check (`checkDeadline`) only runs **between** lines/blocks, never inside `pattern.hasMatch`, so a single pathological match on one giant record wedges the tool call — and the cancel token is not consulted during `execute` either — far beyond the promised 10 s, producing a hung agent rather than an "honest `truncated` report".

This matters more here than for a plain grep tool because the regex comes from the model itself, which routinely emits accidentally-quadratic patterns, and this PR's headline scenario is giant records.

Directions: bound the regex subject far smaller (a match over the first N KB of the record's preview-sized excerpt is enough for a pointer), or run the match in an isolate that can be abandoned on deadline expiry, or explicitly scope the E5 claim down to "budget checked between records" and cap per-record regex input accordingly.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment07.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: accumulator state grows linearly with archive size — the flat-memory claim (E4) does not hold**

`scanSessionSegment`'s doc claims "memory stays flat regardless of file size (E4)", and that is true only for the block/carry streaming. The accumulator itself retains per-record state for the whole chain: `_parentOf` for **every** record id (plus `_ordinalOf` in map mode, doubling it). For a multi-GB archive — this PR's explicit target — with a few million records this is hundreds of MB of id→parent pairs held for the entire scan, and it also accumulates identically on every continuation page.

Directions: the branch walk only needs parents of records on the leaf→root path. Since `RangedReadFileSystem` supports ranged reads, consider a two-pass approach (find the leaf in pass 1 storing only checkpoint/parent facts sparsely, then walk backwards in ranges), or keep parents only for records at/after the last observed fork, or correct the doc comment to state the linear bound honestly and decide whether it is acceptable for the E4 giant-session scenario.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment08.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: the human-readable outcome of `recordPendingWait` is constructed and then discarded**

`recordPendingWait`'s doc says failures are "REPORTED here and swallowed by the afterToolCall wrapper" — but the wrapper (`_attachObligationPendingWaits`) awaits the result and drops it on the floor: nothing is ever reported anywhere, and all the outcome strings (`'pending-wait already recorded…'`, `'did not carry a scheduled id…'`, the swallow-message) are dead text. As written, a silent permanent failure (e.g. the schedule_message result wording changes — see the regex coupling note) is indistinguishable from success.

Either log the outcome through the CLI's logger/bus inside the wrapper, or drop the return value and simplify `recordPendingWait` to `Future<void>` so the code says what it does.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment09.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: only the `result cap` stop carries a continuation token — time-budget stops cannot be paged**

`nextContinuation` is set exclusively when `_stopReason == 'result cap'`. A scan stopped by the 10 s budget mid-archive gets `truncated: true` with no token, so the model's only recourse is the footer advice to narrow with `kinds`/`before`/`after` — fine for specific queries, but for a broad recall sweep over a multi-GB chain there may be no narrowing that fits the budget, and the agent is stuck re-scanning from the start each call (where it will time out again at roughly the same place, since the skip only honors the token).

Since `_skipped` already implements absolute-record skipping, the token is computable for any clean stop: consider `nextContinuation = recordsTotal - 1` (or `recordsTotal`, boundary semantics permitting) whenever the stop was not an error, and extend the footer to offer continuation for `time budget` too.

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the hit cap is counted before the branch-scope filter — the default scope under-delivers and pages O(n²)**

`seeRecord` stops at `query.maxHits` hits in `_hits`, but `finish()` only then filters to the active branch. Since `branch` is the **default** scope, every match on an abandoned fork consumes budget and can trigger a premature `result cap` that returns far fewer than 40 branch hits — or zero — while reporting `truncated: true`. Worse, the continuation token skips records globally, so each next page re-scans the entire prefix of the chain: paging through a fork-heavy giant session is O(n²) under a 10 s budget.

No test covers branch-scope + cap together (the seeded fork record doesn't match the test query, so the E4 test can't see this).

Directions: collect hits with branch membership decided at collection time where possible, or over-collect with slack and continue scanning when the branch-filtered count is below the cap; alternatively exclude non-branch hits from the cap accounting and document that a capped branch scan may re-examine fork hits on the next page.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment06.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the E5 "never a hang" guarantee is not enforceable — one record can blow the wall-clock budget**

The comment frames this cap as the E5 DoS bound, but a text-length cap is not a time bound on a backtracking regex engine (the Dart VM's `RegExp` backtracks — catastrophic patterns like `(a+)+$` over the 128 KB record are effectively unbounded). The time-budget check (`checkDeadline`) only runs **between** lines/blocks, never inside `pattern.hasMatch`, so a single pathological match on one giant record wedges the tool call — and the cancel token is not consulted during `execute` either — far beyond the promised 10 s, producing a hung agent rather than an "honest `truncated` report".

This matters more here than for a plain grep tool because the regex comes from the model itself, which routinely emits accidentally-quadratic patterns, and this PR's headline scenario is giant records.

Directions: bound the regex subject far smaller (a match over the first N KB of the record's preview-sized excerpt is enough for a pointer), or run the match in an isolate that can be abandoned on deadline expiry, or explicitly scope the E5 claim down to "budget checked between records" and cap per-record regex input accordingly.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment07.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: accumulator state grows linearly with archive size — the flat-memory claim (E4) does not hold**

`scanSessionSegment`'s doc claims "memory stays flat regardless of file size (E4)", and that is true only for the block/carry streaming. The accumulator itself retains per-record state for the whole chain: `_parentOf` for **every** record id (plus `_ordinalOf` in map mode, doubling it). For a multi-GB archive — this PR's explicit target — with a few million records this is hundreds of MB of id→parent pairs held for the entire scan, and it also accumulates identically on every continuation page.

Directions: the branch walk only needs parents of records on the leaf→root path. Since `RangedReadFileSystem` supports ranged reads, consider a two-pass approach (find the leaf in pass 1 storing only checkpoint/parent facts sparsely, then walk backwards in ranges), or keep parents only for records at/after the last observed fork, or correct the doc comment to state the linear bound honestly and decide whether it is acceptable for the E4 giant-session scenario.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment08.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: the human-readable outcome of `recordPendingWait` is constructed and then discarded**

`recordPendingWait`'s doc says failures are "REPORTED here and swallowed by the afterToolCall wrapper" — but the wrapper (`_attachObligationPendingWaits`) awaits the result and drops it on the floor: nothing is ever reported anywhere, and all the outcome strings (`'pending-wait already recorded…'`, `'did not carry a scheduled id…'`, the swallow-message) are dead text. As written, a silent permanent failure (e.g. the schedule_message result wording changes — see the regex coupling note) is indistinguishable from success.

Either log the outcome through the CLI's logger/bus inside the wrapper, or drop the return value and simplify `recordPendingWait` to `Future<void>` so the code says what it does.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment09.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: only the `result cap` stop carries a continuation token — time-budget stops cannot be paged**

`nextContinuation` is set exclusively when `_stopReason == 'result cap'`. A scan stopped by the 10 s budget mid-archive gets `truncated: true` with no token, so the model's only recourse is the footer advice to narrow with `kinds`/`before`/`after` — fine for specific queries, but for a broad recall sweep over a multi-GB chain there may be no narrowing that fits the budget, and the agent is stuck re-scanning from the start each call (where it will time out again at roughly the same place, since the skip only honors the token).

Since `_skipped` already implements absolute-record skipping, the token is computable for any clean stop: consider `nextContinuation = recordsTotal - 1` (or `recordsTotal`, boundary semantics permitting) whenever the stop was not an error, and extend the footer to offer continuation for `time budget` too.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment11.md"}

All required context — ticket description, PR diff, CI status, and related materials — has already been prepared in the `input/` folder. Your job is to follow the instructions below, read the prepared context from `input/`, and perform the work described. Do not ask for identifiers; the context is already available locally. ```mermaid flowchart TD G1["⚠️ Review Guidelines — evaluate against existing codebase patterns"] G2["Before reviewing, explore the project's code structure, architecture, and testing patterns"] G3["If AGENTS.md exists → READ it — defines coding styles to check against"] G4["Flag deviations from established patterns unless justified in PR description"] G1 --> G2 --> G3 --> G4 ``` # PR Review General Guidelines ## Review flow ```mermaid flowchart TD START([PR ready for review]) --> READ["1. Read input context:
instruction.md, ticket.md, pr_info.md,
pr_diff.txt, pr_files.txt, ci_failures.md,

pr_discussions_raw.json"] READ --> DIFF["2. Run diff checklist on pr_diff.txt"] DIFF --> FILES["3. Read full content of every changed file"] FILES --> CODEGRAPH["4. Use CodeGraph:
callers/callees of changed symbols,
search for sensitive patterns,
impact analysis"] CODEGRAPH --> DIMS["5. Evaluate review dimensions:
Security · Architecture/OOP · Code quality
Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. Outputs Write the standard review artifacts: - `outputs/pr_review.json` — structured data with `recommendation`, `summary`, `inlineComments`, `issueCounts` - `outputs/pr_review_general.md` — 1-2 paragraph general PR comment - `outputs/pr_review_comments/*.md` — one file per detailed inline comment **Inline comment lines must be present in the PR diff.** GitHub review threads can only be attached to added or context lines inside a diff hunk. {"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the "no session file" degradation renders as "no records match" — the graceful-null contract is dishonest in practice**

When the host has no backing session file, this returns `truncated: false, truncationReason: 'no session file'` with zero totals. But `formatSessionSearchOutcome` only surfaces `truncationReason` when `truncated` is true, so the model actually sees:

```text
no records match (examined 0 of 0 records)
```

That claims the archive was scanned and is empty — the opposite of "this host cannot search". The tool-level null-callback branch (`'This host has no session file to search.'`) is never reached from the CLI because the callback is always `searchSessionArchive`. This contradicts the PR's stated "degrades to the same graceful cannot-execute result as ask/request_secret".

Fix options: give `SessionSearchOutcome` a dedicated `unavailableReason` that the formatter prints verbatim, or return `truncated: true` here with the reason (the footer path already prints it). Add a tool-level test that runs the formatter against exactly this outcome.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment05.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the hit cap is counted before the branch-scope filter — the default scope under-delivers and pages O(n²)**

`seeRecord` stops at `query.maxHits` hits in `_hits`, but `finish()` only then filters to the active branch. Since `branch` is the **default** scope, every match on an abandoned fork consumes budget and can trigger a premature `result cap` that returns far fewer than 40 branch hits — or zero — while reporting `truncated: true`. Worse, the continuation token skips records globally, so each next page re-scans the entire prefix of the chain: paging through a fork-heavy giant session is O(n²) under a 10 s budget.

No test covers branch-scope + cap together (the seeded fork record doesn't match the test query, so the E4 test can't see this).

Directions: collect hits with branch membership decided at collection time where possible, or over-collect with slack and continue scanning when the branch-filtered count is below the cap; alternatively exclude non-branch hits from the cap accounting and document that a capped branch scan may re-examine fork hits on the next page.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment06.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the E5 "never a hang" guarantee is not enforceable — one record can blow the wall-clock budget**

The comment frames this cap as the E5 DoS bound, but a text-length cap is not a time bound on a backtracking regex engine (the Dart VM's `RegExp` backtracks — catastrophic patterns like `(a+)+$` over the 128 KB record are effectively unbounded). The time-budget check (`checkDeadline`) only runs **between** lines/blocks, never inside `pattern.hasMatch`, so a single pathological match on one giant record wedges the tool call — and the cancel token is not consulted during `execute` either — far beyond the promised 10 s, producing a hung agent rather than an "honest `truncated` report".

This matters more here than for a plain grep tool because the regex comes from the model itself, which routinely emits accidentally-quadratic patterns, and this PR's headline scenario is giant records.

Directions: bound the regex subject far smaller (a match over the first N KB of the record's preview-sized excerpt is enough for a pointer), or run the match in an isolate that can be abandoned on deadline expiry, or explicitly scope the E5 claim down to "budget checked between records" and cap per-record regex input accordingly.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment07.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: accumulator state grows linearly with archive size — the flat-memory claim (E4) does not hold**

`scanSessionSegment`'s doc claims "memory stays flat regardless of file size (E4)", and that is true only for the block/carry streaming. The accumulator itself retains per-record state for the whole chain: `_parentOf` for **every** record id (plus `_ordinalOf` in map mode, doubling it). For a multi-GB archive — this PR's explicit target — with a few million records this is hundreds of MB of id→parent pairs held for the entire scan, and it also accumulates identically on every continuation page.

Directions: the branch walk only needs parents of records on the leaf→root path. Since `RangedReadFileSystem` supports ranged reads, consider a two-pass approach (find the leaf in pass 1 storing only checkpoint/parent facts sparsely, then walk backwards in ranges), or keep parents only for records at/after the last observed fork, or correct the doc comment to state the linear bound honestly and decide whether it is acceptable for the E4 giant-session scenario.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment08.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: the human-readable outcome of `recordPendingWait` is constructed and then discarded**

`recordPendingWait`'s doc says failures are "REPORTED here and swallowed by the afterToolCall wrapper" — but the wrapper (`_attachObligationPendingWaits`) awaits the result and drops it on the floor: nothing is ever reported anywhere, and all the outcome strings (`'pending-wait already recorded…'`, `'did not carry a scheduled id…'`, the swallow-message) are dead text. As written, a silent permanent failure (e.g. the schedule_message result wording changes — see the regex coupling note) is indistinguishable from success.

Either log the outcome through the CLI's logger/bus inside the wrapper, or drop the return value and simplify `recordPendingWait` to `Future<void>` so the code says what it does.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment09.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: only the `result cap` stop carries a continuation token — time-budget stops cannot be paged**

`nextContinuation` is set exclusively when `_stopReason == 'result cap'`. A scan stopped by the 10 s budget mid-archive gets `truncated: true` with no token, so the model's only recourse is the footer advice to narrow with `kinds`/`before`/`after` — fine for specific queries, but for a broad recall sweep over a multi-GB chain there may be no narrowing that fits the budget, and the agent is stuck re-scanning from the start each call (where it will time out again at roughly the same place, since the skip only honors the token).

Since `_skipped` already implements absolute-record skipping, the token is computable for any clean stop: consider `nextContinuation = recordsTotal - 1` (or `recordsTotal`, boundary semantics permitting) whenever the stop was not an error, and extend the footer to offer continuation for `time budget` too.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment11.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the hit cap is counted before the branch-scope filter — the default scope under-delivers and pages O(n²)**

`seeRecord` stops at `query.maxHits` hits in `_hits`, but `finish()` only then filters to the active branch. Since `branch` is the **default** scope, every match on an abandoned fork consumes budget and can trigger a premature `result cap` that returns far fewer than 40 branch hits — or zero — while reporting `truncated: true`. Worse, the continuation token skips records globally, so each next page re-scans the entire prefix of the chain: paging through a fork-heavy giant session is O(n²) under a 10 s budget.

No test covers branch-scope + cap together (the seeded fork record doesn't match the test query, so the E4 test can't see this).

Directions: collect hits with branch membership decided at collection time where possible, or over-collect with slack and continue scanning when the branch-filtered count is below the cap; alternatively exclude non-branch hits from the cap accounting and document that a capped branch scan may re-examine fork hits on the next page.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment06.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the E5 "never a hang" guarantee is not enforceable — one record can blow the wall-clock budget**

The comment frames this cap as the E5 DoS bound, but a text-length cap is not a time bound on a backtracking regex engine (the Dart VM's `RegExp` backtracks — catastrophic patterns like `(a+)+$` over the 128 KB record are effectively unbounded). The time-budget check (`checkDeadline`) only runs **between** lines/blocks, never inside `pattern.hasMatch`, so a single pathological match on one giant record wedges the tool call — and the cancel token is not consulted during `execute` either — far beyond the promised 10 s, producing a hung agent rather than an "honest `truncated` report".

This matters more here than for a plain grep tool because the regex comes from the model itself, which routinely emits accidentally-quadratic patterns, and this PR's headline scenario is giant records.

Directions: bound the regex subject far smaller (a match over the first N KB of the record's preview-sized excerpt is enough for a pointer), or run the match in an isolate that can be abandoned on deadline expiry, or explicitly scope the E5 claim down to "budget checked between records" and cap per-record regex input accordingly.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment07.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: accumulator state grows linearly with archive size — the flat-memory claim (E4) does not hold**

`scanSessionSegment`'s doc claims "memory stays flat regardless of file size (E4)", and that is true only for the block/carry streaming. The accumulator itself retains per-record state for the whole chain: `_parentOf` for **every** record id (plus `_ordinalOf` in map mode, doubling it). For a multi-GB archive — this PR's explicit target — with a few million records this is hundreds of MB of id→parent pairs held for the entire scan, and it also accumulates identically on every continuation page.

Directions: the branch walk only needs parents of records on the leaf→root path. Since `RangedReadFileSystem` supports ranged reads, consider a two-pass approach (find the leaf in pass 1 storing only checkpoint/parent facts sparsely, then walk backwards in ranges), or keep parents only for records at/after the last observed fork, or correct the doc comment to state the linear bound honestly and decide whether it is acceptable for the E4 giant-session scenario.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment08.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: the human-readable outcome of `recordPendingWait` is constructed and then discarded**

`recordPendingWait`'s doc says failures are "REPORTED here and swallowed by the afterToolCall wrapper" — but the wrapper (`_attachObligationPendingWaits`) awaits the result and drops it on the floor: nothing is ever reported anywhere, and all the outcome strings (`'pending-wait already recorded…'`, `'did not carry a scheduled id…'`, the swallow-message) are dead text. As written, a silent permanent failure (e.g. the schedule_message result wording changes — see the regex coupling note) is indistinguishable from success.

Either log the outcome through the CLI's logger/bus inside the wrapper, or drop the return value and simplify `recordPendingWait` to `Future<void>` so the code says what it does.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment09.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: only the `result cap` stop carries a continuation token — time-budget stops cannot be paged**

`nextContinuation` is set exclusively when `_stopReason == 'result cap'`. A scan stopped by the 10 s budget mid-archive gets `truncated: true` with no token, so the model's only recourse is the footer advice to narrow with `kinds`/`before`/`after` — fine for specific queries, but for a broad recall sweep over a multi-GB chain there may be no narrowing that fits the budget, and the agent is stuck re-scanning from the start each call (where it will time out again at roughly the same place, since the skip only honors the token).

Since `_skipped` already implements absolute-record skipping, the token is computable for any clean stop: consider `nextContinuation = recordsTotal - 1` (or `recordsTotal`, boundary semantics permitting) whenever the stop was not an error, and extend the footer to offer continuation for `time budget` too.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment11.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the "no session file" degradation renders as "no records match" — the graceful-null contract is dishonest in practice**

When the host has no backing session file, this returns `truncated: false, truncationReason: 'no session file'` with zero totals. But `formatSessionSearchOutcome` only surfaces `truncationReason` when `truncated` is true, so the model actually sees:

```text
no records match (examined 0 of 0 records)
```

That claims the archive was scanned and is empty — the opposite of "this host cannot search". The tool-level null-callback branch (`'This host has no session file to search.'`) is never reached from the CLI because the callback is always `searchSessionArchive`. This contradicts the PR's stated "degrades to the same graceful cannot-execute result as ask/request_secret".

Fix options: give `SessionSearchOutcome` a dedicated `unavailableReason` that the formatter prints verbatim, or return `truncated: true` here with the reason (the footer path already prints it). Add a tool-level test that runs the formatter against exactly this outcome.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment05.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the hit cap is counted before the branch-scope filter — the default scope under-delivers and pages O(n²)**

`seeRecord` stops at `query.maxHits` hits in `_hits`, but `finish()` only then filters to the active branch. Since `branch` is the **default** scope, every match on an abandoned fork consumes budget and can trigger a premature `result cap` that returns far fewer than 40 branch hits — or zero — while reporting `truncated: true`. Worse, the continuation token skips records globally, so each next page re-scans the entire prefix of the chain: paging through a fork-heavy giant session is O(n²) under a 10 s budget.

No test covers branch-scope + cap together (the seeded fork record doesn't match the test query, so the E4 test can't see this).

Directions: collect hits with branch membership decided at collection time where possible, or over-collect with slack and continue scanning when the branch-filtered count is below the cap; alternatively exclude non-branch hits from the cap accounting and document that a capped branch scan may re-examine fork hits on the next page.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment06.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the E5 "never a hang" guarantee is not enforceable — one record can blow the wall-clock budget**

The comment frames this cap as the E5 DoS bound, but a text-length cap is not a time bound on a backtracking regex engine (the Dart VM's `RegExp` backtracks — catastrophic patterns like `(a+)+$` over the 128 KB record are effectively unbounded). The time-budget check (`checkDeadline`) only runs **between** lines/blocks, never inside `pattern.hasMatch`, so a single pathological match on one giant record wedges the tool call — and the cancel token is not consulted during `execute` either — far beyond the promised 10 s, producing a hung agent rather than an "honest `truncated` report".

This matters more here than for a plain grep tool because the regex comes from the model itself, which routinely emits accidentally-quadratic patterns, and this PR's headline scenario is giant records.

Directions: bound the regex subject far smaller (a match over the first N KB of the record's preview-sized excerpt is enough for a pointer), or run the match in an isolate that can be abandoned on deadline expiry, or explicitly scope the E5 claim down to "budget checked between records" and cap per-record regex input accordingly.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment07.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: accumulator state grows linearly with archive size — the flat-memory claim (E4) does not hold**

`scanSessionSegment`'s doc claims "memory stays flat regardless of file size (E4)", and that is true only for the block/carry streaming. The accumulator itself retains per-record state for the whole chain: `_parentOf` for **every** record id (plus `_ordinalOf` in map mode, doubling it). For a multi-GB archive — this PR's explicit target — with a few million records this is hundreds of MB of id→parent pairs held for the entire scan, and it also accumulates identically on every continuation page.

Directions: the branch walk only needs parents of records on the leaf→root path. Since `RangedReadFileSystem` supports ranged reads, consider a two-pass approach (find the leaf in pass 1 storing only checkpoint/parent facts sparsely, then walk backwards in ranges), or keep parents only for records at/after the last observed fork, or correct the doc comment to state the linear bound honestly and decide whether it is acceptable for the E4 giant-session scenario.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment08.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: the human-readable outcome of `recordPendingWait` is constructed and then discarded**

`recordPendingWait`'s doc says failures are "REPORTED here and swallowed by the afterToolCall wrapper" — but the wrapper (`_attachObligationPendingWaits`) awaits the result and drops it on the floor: nothing is ever reported anywhere, and all the outcome strings (`'pending-wait already recorded…'`, `'did not carry a scheduled id…'`, the swallow-message) are dead text. As written, a silent permanent failure (e.g. the schedule_message result wording changes — see the regex coupling note) is indistinguishable from success.

Either log the outcome through the CLI's logger/bus inside the wrapper, or drop the return value and simplify `recordPendingWait` to `Future<void>` so the code says what it does.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment09.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: only the `result cap` stop carries a continuation token — time-budget stops cannot be paged**

`nextContinuation` is set exclusively when `_stopReason == 'result cap'`. A scan stopped by the 10 s budget mid-archive gets `truncated: true` with no token, so the model's only recourse is the footer advice to narrow with `kinds`/`before`/`after` — fine for specific queries, but for a broad recall sweep over a multi-GB chain there may be no narrowing that fits the budget, and the agent is stuck re-scanning from the start each call (where it will time out again at roughly the same place, since the skip only honors the token).

Since `_skipped` already implements absolute-record skipping, the token is computable for any clean stop: consider `nextContinuation = recordsTotal - 1` (or `recordsTotal`, boundary semantics permitting) whenever the stop was not an error, and extend the footer to offer continuation for `time budget` too.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment11.md"}

Correct: if group body contains quantified atom → group has quantified body. Yes.
   - But there's a subtle bug: when a group closes, `lastGroupHasQuantified` is set. But if the NEXT char is not a quantifier, lastGroupHasQuantified remains stale... e.g. `(a+)b` — at `)`, lastGroupHasQuantified=true, lastAtomWasGroup=true. At `b` → default: lastAtomWasGroup=false. OK reset.
   - `(a+)+` → `(` push false; `a` default resets; `+` marks group last=true, lastAtomQuantified=true; `)` pops → lastGroupHasQuantified=true, lastAtomWasGroup=true; `+` → lastAtomWasGroup && lastGroupHasQuantified → true.

   - What about `(a+)+?` — lazy modifier: `+` after group → return true at the second `+`. Fine.

So `((a+))+` passes the screen but is catastrophic. False negatives exist. But the doc says ambiguous shapes not screened; nested groups shape... The honest doc says residual is scoped & documented ("one unscreened pathological match ... can still exceed the budget; that residual is scoped, documented"). Still, `((a+))+` is precisely the "(a+)+-shape" the error message names, just wrapped — a model could easily produce it. Is this worth a SUGGESTION/IMPORTANT? The screen is best-effort with documented residual. False negatives for doubly-nested groups is a reasonable limitation; but since the parse-time rejection is the headline E5 defense, a note could be added. I'd file this as SUGGESTION: propagate the "contains quantified group" fact outward so `((a+))+` is also rejected, or extend the error message. Actually wait — also check `(a*)*` etc. Similar. And what about `(?:a+)+`? `(` at i, pattern[i+1]=='?' → i++ (skips '?'); then `a` default, `+` marks top group true, `)` pops → lastGroupHasQuantified=true, `+` → detected. Good.

But what about `??`? first `?`: lastAtomQuantified false (e.g. after `a`)... wait `a??` — `a` default → lastAtomQuantified=false; `?` → not lastAtomQuantified → sets lastAtomQuantified=true, marks group. Second `?` → lastAtomQuantified true → lazy → break. OK.

The deadline is shared (`deadline = now + budget` computed once, passed to both accumulators). So the census consumes part of the budget, then the real pass gets the remainder. Is this flagged? The docstring says "Map mode and branch scope pay one extra read-only census pass first". The 10s budget is shared across both passes, which is at least honest about wall clock. And the census pass re-runs completely on every page (no continuation skip in census — census.seeRecord doesn't handle query.continuation... it counts recordsTotal and returns; no skip logic. So the census scans the entire chain every page). So paging a giant session is O(pages × full chain) — for page 10 of a 1GB archive that's 10 full reads. So paging behavior unchanged in asymptotic terms; the census adds a constant 2x per page. The finding said paging is O(n²) under a 10s budget; the fix addresses the cap-under-delivery, not the O(n²) paging. {"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the hit cap is counted before the branch-scope filter — the default scope under-delivers and pages O(n²)**

`seeRecord` stops at `query.maxHits` hits in `_hits`, but `finish()` only then filters to the active branch. Since `branch` is the **default** scope, every match on an abandoned fork consumes budget and can trigger a premature `result cap` that returns far fewer than 40 branch hits — or zero — while reporting `truncated: true`. Worse, the continuation token skips records globally, so each next page re-scans the entire prefix of the chain: paging through a fork-heavy giant session is O(n²) under a 10 s budget.

No test covers branch-scope + cap together (the seeded fork record doesn't match the test query, so the E4 test can't see this).

Directions: collect hits with branch membership decided at collection time where possible, or over-collect with slack and continue scanning when the branch-filtered count is below the cap; alternatively exclude non-branch hits from the cap accounting and document that a capped branch scan may re-examine fork hits on the next page.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment06.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the E5 "never a hang" guarantee is not enforceable — one record can blow the wall-clock budget**

The comment frames this cap as the E5 DoS bound, but a text-length cap is not a time bound on a backtracking regex engine (the Dart VM's `RegExp` backtracks — catastrophic patterns like `(a+)+$` over the 128 KB record are effectively unbounded). The time-budget check (`checkDeadline`) only runs **between** lines/blocks, never inside `pattern.hasMatch`, so a single pathological match on one giant record wedges the tool call — and the cancel token is not consulted during `execute` either — far beyond the promised 10 s, producing a hung agent rather than an "honest `truncated` report".

This matters more here than for a plain grep tool because the regex comes from the model itself, which routinely emits accidentally-quadratic patterns, and this PR's headline scenario is giant records.

Directions: bound the regex subject far smaller (a match over the first N KB of the record's preview-sized excerpt is enough for a pointer), or run the match in an isolate that can be abandoned on deadline expiry, or explicitly scope the E5 claim down to "budget checked between records" and cap per-record regex input accordingly.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment07.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: accumulator state grows linearly with archive size — the flat-memory claim (E4) does not hold**

`scanSessionSegment`'s doc claims "memory stays flat regardless of file size (E4)", and that is true only for the block/carry streaming. The accumulator itself retains per-record state for the whole chain: `_parentOf` for **every** record id (plus `_ordinalOf` in map mode, doubling it). For a multi-GB archive — this PR's explicit target — with a few million records this is hundreds of MB of id→parent pairs held for the entire scan, and it also accumulates identically on every continuation page.

Directions: the branch walk only needs parents of records on the leaf→root path. Since `RangedReadFileSystem` supports ranged reads, consider a two-pass approach (find the leaf in pass 1 storing only checkpoint/parent facts sparsely, then walk backwards in ranges), or keep parents only for records at/after the last observed fork, or correct the doc comment to state the linear bound honestly and decide whether it is acceptable for the E4 giant-session scenario.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment08.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: the human-readable outcome of `recordPendingWait` is constructed and then discarded**

`recordPendingWait`'s doc says failures are "REPORTED here and swallowed by the afterToolCall wrapper" — but the wrapper (`_attachObligationPendingWaits`) awaits the result and drops it on the floor: nothing is ever reported anywhere, and all the outcome strings (`'pending-wait already recorded…'`, `'did not carry a scheduled id…'`, the swallow-message) are dead text. As written, a silent permanent failure (e.g. the schedule_message result wording changes — see the regex coupling note) is indistinguishable from success.

Either log the outcome through the CLI's logger/bus inside the wrapper, or drop the return value and simplify `recordPendingWait` to `Future<void>` so the code says what it does.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment09.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: only the `result cap` stop carries a continuation token — time-budget stops cannot be paged**

`nextContinuation` is set exclusively when `_stopReason == 'result cap'`. A scan stopped by the 10 s budget mid-archive gets `truncated: true` with no token, so the model's only recourse is the footer advice to narrow with `kinds`/`before`/`after` — fine for specific queries, but for a broad recall sweep over a multi-GB chain there may be no narrowing that fits the budget, and the agent is stuck re-scanning from the start each call (where it will time out again at roughly the same place, since the skip only honors the token).

Since `_skipped` already implements absolute-record skipping, the token is computable for any clean stop: consider `nextContinuation = recordsTotal - 1` (or `recordsTotal`, boundary semantics permitting) whenever the stop was not an error, and extend the footer to offer continuation for `time budget` too.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment11.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the "no session file" degradation renders as "no records match" — the graceful-null contract is dishonest in practice**

When the host has no backing session file, this returns `truncated: false, truncationReason: 'no session file'` with zero totals. But `formatSessionSearchOutcome` only surfaces `truncationReason` when `truncated` is true, so the model actually sees:

```text
no records match (examined 0 of 0 records)
```

That claims the archive was scanned and is empty — the opposite of "this host cannot search". The tool-level null-callback branch (`'This host has no session file to search.'`) is never reached from the CLI because the callback is always `searchSessionArchive`. This contradicts the PR's stated "degrades to the same graceful cannot-execute result as ask/request_secret".

Fix options: give `SessionSearchOutcome` a dedicated `unavailableReason` that the formatter prints verbatim, or return `truncated: true` here with the reason (the footer path already prints it). Add a tool-level test that runs the formatter against exactly this outcome.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment05.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the hit cap is counted before the branch-scope filter — the default scope under-delivers and pages O(n²)**

`seeRecord` stops at `query.maxHits` hits in `_hits`, but `finish()` only then filters to the active branch. Since `branch` is the **default** scope, every match on an abandoned fork consumes budget and can trigger a premature `result cap` that returns far fewer than 40 branch hits — or zero — while reporting `truncated: true`. Worse, the continuation token skips records globally, so each next page re-scans the entire prefix of the chain: paging through a fork-heavy giant session is O(n²) under a 10 s budget.

No test covers branch-scope + cap together (the seeded fork record doesn't match the test query, so the E4 test can't see this).

Directions: collect hits with branch membership decided at collection time where possible, or over-collect with slack and continue scanning when the branch-filtered count is below the cap; alternatively exclude non-branch hits from the cap accounting and document that a capped branch scan may re-examine fork hits on the next page.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment06.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the E5 "never a hang" guarantee is not enforceable — one record can blow the wall-clock budget**

The comment frames this cap as the E5 DoS bound, but a text-length cap is not a time bound on a backtracking regex engine (the Dart VM's `RegExp` backtracks — catastrophic patterns like `(a+)+$` over the 128 KB record are effectively unbounded). The time-budget check (`checkDeadline`) only runs **between** lines/blocks, never inside `pattern.hasMatch`, so a single pathological match on one giant record wedges the tool call — and the cancel token is not consulted during `execute` either — far beyond the promised 10 s, producing a hung agent rather than an "honest `truncated` report".

This matters more here than for a plain grep tool because the regex comes from the model itself, which routinely emits accidentally-quadratic patterns, and this PR's headline scenario is giant records.

Directions: bound the regex subject far smaller (a match over the first N KB of the record's preview-sized excerpt is enough for a pointer), or run the match in an isolate that can be abandoned on deadline expiry, or explicitly scope the E5 claim down to "budget checked between records" and cap per-record regex input accordingly.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment07.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: accumulator state grows linearly with archive size — the flat-memory claim (E4) does not hold**

`scanSessionSegment`'s doc claims "memory stays flat regardless of file size (E4)", and that is true only for the block/carry streaming. The accumulator itself retains per-record state for the whole chain: `_parentOf` for **every** record id (plus `_ordinalOf` in map mode, doubling it). For a multi-GB archive — this PR's explicit target — with a few million records this is hundreds of MB of id→parent pairs held for the entire scan, and it also accumulates identically on every continuation page.

Directions: the branch walk only needs parents of records on the leaf→root path. Since `RangedReadFileSystem` supports ranged reads, consider a two-pass approach (find the leaf in pass 1 storing only checkpoint/parent facts sparsely, then walk backwards in ranges), or keep parents only for records at/after the last observed fork, or correct the doc comment to state the linear bound honestly and decide whether it is acceptable for the E4 giant-session scenario.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment08.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: the human-readable outcome of `recordPendingWait` is constructed and then discarded**

`recordPendingWait`'s doc says failures are "REPORTED here and swallowed by the afterToolCall wrapper" — but the wrapper (`_attachObligationPendingWaits`) awaits the result and drops it on the floor: nothing is ever reported anywhere, and all the outcome strings (`'pending-wait already recorded…'`, `'did not carry a scheduled id…'`, the swallow-message) are dead text. As written, a silent permanent failure (e.g. the schedule_message result wording changes — see the regex coupling note) is indistinguishable from success.

Either log the outcome through the CLI's logger/bus inside the wrapper, or drop the return value and simplify `recordPendingWait` to `Future<void>` so the code says what it does.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment09.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: only the `result cap` stop carries a continuation token — time-budget stops cannot be paged**

`nextContinuation` is set exclusively when `_stopReason == 'result cap'`. A scan stopped by the 10 s budget mid-archive gets `truncated: true` with no token, so the model's only recourse is the footer advice to narrow with `kinds`/`before`/`after` — fine for specific queries, but for a broad recall sweep over a multi-GB chain there may be no narrowing that fits the budget, and the agent is stuck re-scanning from the start each call (where it will time out again at roughly the same place, since the skip only honors the token).

Since `_skipped` already implements absolute-record skipping, the token is computable for any clean stop: consider `nextContinuation = recordsTotal - 1` (or `recordsTotal`, boundary semantics permitting) whenever the stop was not an error, and extend the footer to offer continuation for `time budget` too.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment11.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the hit cap is counted before the branch-scope filter — the default scope under-delivers and pages O(n²)**

`seeRecord` stops at `query.maxHits` hits in `_hits`, but `finish()` only then filters to the active branch. Since `branch` is the **default** scope, every match on an abandoned fork consumes budget and can trigger a premature `result cap` that returns far fewer than 40 branch hits — or zero — while reporting `truncated: true`. Worse, the continuation token skips records globally, so each next page re-scans the entire prefix of the chain: paging through a fork-heavy giant session is O(n²) under a 10 s budget.

No test covers branch-scope + cap together (the seeded fork record doesn't match the test query, so the E4 test can't see this).

Directions: collect hits with branch membership decided at collection time where possible, or over-collect with slack and continue scanning when the branch-filtered count is below the cap; alternatively exclude non-branch hits from the cap accounting and document that a capped branch scan may re-examine fork hits on the next page.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment06.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the E5 "never a hang" guarantee is not enforceable — one record can blow the wall-clock budget**

The comment frames this cap as the E5 DoS bound, but a text-length cap is not a time bound on a backtracking regex engine (the Dart VM's `RegExp` backtracks — catastrophic patterns like `(a+)+$` over the 128 KB record are effectively unbounded). The time-budget check (`checkDeadline`) only runs **between** lines/blocks, never inside `pattern.hasMatch`, so a single pathological match on one giant record wedges the tool call — and the cancel token is not consulted during `execute` either — far beyond the promised 10 s, producing a hung agent rather than an "honest `truncated` report".

This matters more here than for a plain grep tool because the regex comes from the model itself, which routinely emits accidentally-quadratic patterns, and this PR's headline scenario is giant records.

Directions: bound the regex subject far smaller (a match over the first N KB of the record's preview-sized excerpt is enough for a pointer), or run the match in an isolate that can be abandoned on deadline expiry, or explicitly scope the E5 claim down to "budget checked between records" and cap per-record regex input accordingly.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment07.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: accumulator state grows linearly with archive size — the flat-memory claim (E4) does not hold**

`scanSessionSegment`'s doc claims "memory stays flat regardless of file size (E4)", and that is true only for the block/carry streaming. The accumulator itself retains per-record state for the whole chain: `_parentOf` for **every** record id (plus `_ordinalOf` in map mode, doubling it). For a multi-GB archive — this PR's explicit target — with a few million records this is hundreds of MB of id→parent pairs held for the entire scan, and it also accumulates identically on every continuation page.

Directions: the branch walk only needs parents of records on the leaf→root path. Since `RangedReadFileSystem` supports ranged reads, consider a two-pass approach (find the leaf in pass 1 storing only checkpoint/parent facts sparsely, then walk backwards in ranges), or keep parents only for records at/after the last observed fork, or correct the doc comment to state the linear bound honestly and decide whether it is acceptable for the E4 giant-session scenario.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment08.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: the human-readable outcome of `recordPendingWait` is constructed and then discarded**

`recordPendingWait`'s doc says failures are "REPORTED here and swallowed by the afterToolCall wrapper" — but the wrapper (`_attachObligationPendingWaits`) awaits the result and drops it on the floor: nothing is ever reported anywhere, and all the outcome strings (`'pending-wait already recorded…'`, `'did not carry a scheduled id…'`, the swallow-message) are dead text. As written, a silent permanent failure (e.g. the schedule_message result wording changes — see the regex coupling note) is indistinguishable from success.

Either log the outcome through the CLI's logger/bus inside the wrapper, or drop the return value and simplify `recordPendingWait` to `Future<void>` so the code says what it does.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment09.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: only the `result cap` stop carries a continuation token — time-budget stops cannot be paged**

`nextContinuation` is set exclusively when `_stopReason == 'result cap'`. A scan stopped by the 10 s budget mid-archive gets `truncated: true` with no token, so the model's only recourse is the footer advice to narrow with `kinds`/`before`/`after` — fine for specific queries, but for a broad recall sweep over a multi-GB chain there may be no narrowing that fits the budget, and the agent is stuck re-scanning from the start each call (where it will time out again at roughly the same place, since the skip only honors the token).

`seeRecord` stops at `query.maxHits` hits in `_hits`, but `finish()` only then filters to the active branch. Since `branch` is the **default** scope, every match on an abandoned fork consumes budget and can trigger a premature `result cap` that returns far fewer than 40 branch hits — or zero — while reporting `truncated: true`. Worse, the continuation token skips records globally, so each next page re-scans the entire prefix of the chain: paging through a fork-heavy giant session is O(n²) under a 10 s budget.

No test covers branch-scope + cap together (the seeded fork record doesn't match the test query, so the E4 test can't see this).

Directions: collect hits with branch membership decided at collection time where possible, or over-collect with slack and continue scanning when the branch-filtered count is below the cap; alternatively exclude non-branch hits from the cap accounting and document that a capped branch scan may re-examine fork hits on the next page.

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the E5 "never a hang" guarantee is not enforceable — one record can blow the wall-clock budget**

The comment frames this cap as the E5 DoS bound, but a text-length cap is not a time bound on a backtracking regex engine (the Dart VM's `RegExp` backtracks — catastrophic patterns like `(a+)+$` over the 128 KB record are effectively unbounded). The time-budget check (`checkDeadline`) only runs **between** lines/blocks, never inside `pattern.hasMatch`, so a single pathological match on one giant record wedges the tool call — and the cancel token is not consulted during `execute` either — far beyond the promised 10 s, producing a hung agent rather than an "honest `truncated` report".

This matters more here than for a plain grep tool because the regex comes from the model itself, which routinely emits accidentally-quadratic patterns, and this PR's headline scenario is giant records.

Directions: bound the regex subject far smaller (a match over the first N KB of the record's preview-sized excerpt is enough for a pointer), or run the match in an isolate that can be abandoned on deadline expiry, or explicitly scope the E5 claim down to "budget checked between records" and cap per-record regex input accordingly.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment07.md"}

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: accumulator state grows linearly with archive size — the flat-memory claim (E4) does not hold**

`scanSessionSegment`'s doc claims "memory stays flat regardless of file size (E4)", and that is true only for the block/carry streaming. The accumulator itself retains per-record state for the whole chain: `_parentOf` for **every** record id (plus `_ordinalOf` in map mode, doubling it). For a multi-GB archive — this PR's explicit target — with a few million records this is hundreds of MB of id→parent pairs held for the entire scan, and it also accumulates identically on every continuation page.

Directions: the branch walk only needs parents of records on the leaf→root path. Since `RangedReadFileSystem` supports ranged reads, consider a two-pass approach (find the leaf in pass 1 storing only checkpoint/parent facts sparsely, then walk backwards in ranges), or keep parents only for records at/after the last observed fork, or correct the doc comment to state the linear bound honestly and decide whether it is acceptable for the E4 giant-session scenario.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment08.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: the human-readable outcome of `recordPendingWait` is constructed and then discarded**

`recordPendingWait`'s doc says failures are "REPORTED here and swallowed by the afterToolCall wrapper" — but the wrapper (`_attachObligationPendingWaits`) awaits the result and drops it on the floor: nothing is ever reported anywhere, and all the outcome strings (`'pending-wait already recorded…'`, `'did not carry a scheduled id…'`, the swallow-message) are dead text. As written, a silent permanent failure (e.g. the schedule_message result wording changes — see the regex coupling note) is indistinguishable from success.

Either log the outcome through the CLI's logger/bus inside the wrapper, or drop the return value and simplify `recordPendingWait` to `Future<void>` so the code says what it does.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment09.md"}

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: only the `result cap` stop carries a continuation token — time-budget stops cannot be paged**

`nextContinuation` is set exclusively when `_stopReason == 'result cap'`. A scan stopped by the 10 s budget mid-archive gets `truncated: true` with no token, so the model's only recourse is the footer advice to narrow with `kinds`/`before`/`after` — fine for specific queries, but for a broad recall sweep over a multi-GB chain there may be no narrowing that fits the budget, and the agent is stuck re-scanning from the start each call (where it will time out again at roughly the same place, since the skip only honors the token).

Since `_skipped` already implements absolute-record skipping, the token is computable for any clean stop: consider `nextContinuation = recordsTotal - 1` (or `recordsTotal`, boundary semantics permitting) whenever the stop was not an error, and extend the footer to offer continuation for `time budget` too.
","path":"outputs/pr_review_comments/comment11.md"}
